newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - German nationalist Brunner campaigns against EMU.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - German nationalist Brunner campaigns against EMU.

text.p: German newspapers and television ignore him and he is never invited to air his views on radio chat shows.
He was once notorious as Germany's leading opponent of closer European integration -- but soon lapsed into oblivion.
After five years of being consigned to the lunatic fringe, Manfred Brunner is fighting to make a comeback with his crusade to protect the deutschemark.
His main weapons against plans for a single European currency named the "euro" are a fly-leaflet campaign, paid newspaper advertisements and the odd public lecture.
"I'm not opposed to Europe. I'm for a Europe of sovereign states," the portly, bespectacled Brunner told Reuters.

"But I'm convinced the euro will mean the demise of Germany and split Europe asunder. We need different currencies -- they act like shock absorbers during turbulence," he said. "Monetary union would be a national catastrophe."

Brunner, 49, quit Brussels as a senior European Union official in protest against the Maastricht Treaty in 1992 and launched a new right-wing party with a pledge to fight Europe's planned single currency.

Five years ago, when he started out, it was taboo among Bonn's political parties and political establishment to raise doubts about the euro. The few individuals who did were quickly discredited as right-wingers or populists.

But now, more and more mainstream politicians -- notably Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber and potential opposition chancellor candidate Lower Saxony premier Gerhard Schroeder -- are suggesting a delay in the planned 1999 launch of the new currency unit.

But, even now that surveys show most Germans are opposed to giving up the trusty mark for an untested euro, Bonn politicians are careful to stop short of calling for its end -- although commentators suspect this is probably what they want, too.
PAN-EUROPEAN CURRENCY IS "DOOMED"

Convinced that Chancellor Helmut Kohl and his dream of a pan-European currency are doomed, Brunner contends that his Alliance of Free Citizens (BFB) is just the new type of conservative party that Germany needs to fill the "inevitable" void.
Although his party is collecting signatures to petition Bonn to hold a referendum on the euro and has gained 100,000 so far, there is no provision for such a poll in the constitution.
Their chief weapon is a legal challenge and they have set a precedent which other euro-opponents are following.
Brunner challenged the Maastricht Treaty in the Federal Constitutional Court, the highest court in the land, in 1992.

The court ruled a year later that Germany could only adopt a new currency which proved to be as stable as the mark and which showed good prospects for future stability -- a ruling which opponents of a single European currency see as their guarantee of success.

"The constitutional court will prevent currency union or, to avoid a new ruling, the government will delay the project at the end of this year or the beginning of next year," Brunner said. "And when it's delayed -- it's dead!"
BRUNNER DRAWS ON SUPPORT FROM ABROAD

Bonn has been getting cold feet over the euro but does not want to lose face, Brunner argues. The seeds of the euro's failure are already present and lie in France's probable inability to meet the strict Maastricht criteria.

"The Germans will try to give the impression that the French are the culprits. They will say: 'We want the euro but because France has flunked the economic hurdles, the project will unfortunately have to be delayed'," Brunner said.

Brunner has ties with right-wing opponents of increased European integration, or so-called "Eurosceptics", outside Germany, including Austrian far-right leader Joerg Haider, France's Phillipe Devillers and the late Sir James Goldsmith's Referendum Party, which fought in the British election in May.
Political insiders say Brunner's right-wing tendencies might be acceptable elsewhere in Europe but are frowned upon by Germans still haunted by their Nazi past.

"Germans also tend to dismiss Eurosceptics as far-right extremists," said a Bonn-based political correspondent. "No one takes Brunner seriously or his claim he will rescue Germany. He's just a crackpot".
FROM SENIOR EU OFFICIAL TO ANTI-EMU CRUSADER

Once leader of the pro-business Free Democrats (FDP) in Bavaria -- junior coalition partners in Kohl's ruling coalition, Brunner shot into the limelight when he resigned as chef de cabinet to EU Commissioner Martin Bangemann in 1992.
But he failed to win a European Parliament seat two years later to spur his anti-Maastricht campaign and settled for the low-key post of Munich city councillor instead.

Brunner, whose 1,000-member party has a modest base of town councillors in Bavaria and Hesse, as well as regional branches in the rest of Germany's 16 states, took on retired German army colonel Ulrich Quante as his right-hand man and strategist.

Quante has targeted Hamburg, where the next city-state election takes place in September, and is waging a fierce campaign to turn it into a single-issue poll -- one of the last before the key EU decision in spring 1998 on who joins the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
"Our aim is to stop the euro," Quante said. "But even if the euro does not come, it would not mean we had 'won the war'."
"We go beyond that," he said, referring to their programme stressing free-market economics, law and order, low taxes and family values.
